title: Stack-level TCO multiprofile simulations
content:
Purpose:
This spreadsheet-style memo summarizes a set of stack-level cost simulations comparing on-prem (customer-managed datacenter) vs VPC-hosted Private (cloud provider + Private control plane) deployments across multiple workload profiles and support/licensing bundles. It captures assumptions, variable inputs, scenario outputs (3-year NPV-like comparisons), sensitivity pivots, and concrete optimization levers for sales and product to use during pricing conversations and pre-sales sizing.

Scope and audience:
- Audience: sales engineering, solutions engineering, product ops, finance for Private deployments.
- Scope: model-level results for 3 canonical workload profiles (Burst-Interactive, Batch-Heavy, Steady-Low-latency) across 36 months. Includes capital cost and O&M for on-prem, cloud EC2/GPU costs for VPC, licensing + optional premium support bundles.

High-level executive summary (one paragraph):
Across our canonical profiles, VPC generally leads to lower 3-year cash outflow for customers with medium-to-high variability and <36-month hardware refresh cycles due to elasticity and reduced ops staffing. On-prem becomes attractive when customers require >5yr amortization, very predictable steady throughput, and have access to low-cost colocation/power or existing GPU investments. Adding Redwood premium support (24/7 enterprise) increases total cost by 10–18% but materially reduces estimated incident mean time to recovery and adds guaranteed throughput SLOs important to some enterprise customers.

Key assumptions (these are inputs in the sheet, not hard-coded):
- Analysis horizon: 36 months.
- Discount rate / cost of capital: 8% annual (used for NPV-ish adjustments in the sheet).
- On-prem hardware bundle: baseline 8x A100 80GB-equivalent boxes per deployment pod; per-node capital: USD 250k including rack, NV switches, minimal storage.
- Colocation / DC ops: $1,200 / rack-month baseline (varies by region).
- Power and cooling: 25% of colo cost baseline.
- Staffing (on-prem): 2 FTE infra ops + 0.25 SRE support per pod; loaded fully-burdened cost: $250k/FTE/year.
- Cloud (VPC) baseline: GPU hourly price equivalent to on-demand p4d-ish at $3.50/hour per GPU; committed discount simulated by 0%, 30%, 50% (reserved/committed/spot mixes).
- Network egress: 5TB/month baseline; $0.08/GB for heavy egress scenarios.
- Licenses: Redwood Private platform license modeled as flat platform fee + per-GPU seat. Example: $150k platform + $2,000/GPU/month (varied in scenarios).
- Support tiers: Standard (included, email, 8x5), Premium (SLA + 24/7 + prioritized routing) adds 12% of license ARR, Enterprise (SLA + 4hr on-site response option) adds 25% of license ARR.
- Utilization & consolidation: on-prem assumed 40–60% effective utilization w/ tenancy isolation; cloud pooling allows 65–85% utilization for same latency SLOs depending on batching/concurrency.

Model layout (sheet tabs described):
- Inputs: param table with region, GPU type, discount %s, staffing rates, colo costs, license rates, support tier multipliers, utilization assumptions, expected QPS, token throughput, average session length.
- Component costs: per-month breakdown for HW capex amortization, colo rent, power, staffing, spare parts, network, cloud compute, cloud infra services (EBS, LB), Redis caching, logging retention.
- Scenarios: three workload profiles with auto-calculated footprint (GPU count), monthly cost series, cumulative cashflow, and normalized cost-per-1M-inference tokens, cost-per-concurrent-session.
- Sensitivity: one-way sweeps for key drivers (+/- 20–50%): GPU price, utilization, colo rents, support uplift, committed discount.
- Break-even: charts for months-to-breakeven on capex vs commit discount levels, and sensitivity tables for staffing hours and peak utilization.

Representative sample outputs (numbers are illustrative - see sheet for exact cells):
- Burst-Interactive (median case): 3-yr total cost: On-prem $2.45M vs VPC $2.1M assuming 30% reserved discount. Break-even ~28 months if effective utilization diverges >15% in favor of VPC.
- Batch-Heavy (high throughput, tolerant latency): On-prem $1.6M vs VPC $2.05M (on-prem favorable if amortized across 5 yrs; 3-yr horizon still slightly better on-prem if colo and power discounts apply).
- Steady-Low-latency (predictable 24/7): On-prem $3.8M vs VPC $4.0M; on-prem wins if customer already has spare GPU capacity or can amortize hardware >48 months.

Licensing & support bundle recommendations (how we modeled, and suggested packaging):
- Base platform: flat platform fee + per-GPU seat to align cost with GPU scale. This reduces friction for small customers and captures value for large deployments.
- Suggested tiers: Essentials (platform + basic support), Pro (platform + per-GPU + 12% support), Enterprise (platform + per-GPU + 25% support + runbook + canary rollout assistance + monthly architecture review).
- Add-on: On-site installation and training (one-time) vs remote onboarding hours. Price buckets mapped to ARR impact and margin.
- Discount guidance: for customers committing 12–24 months reserved capacity, offer per-GPU discounts in tiers (15% / 30% / 50%) with explicit rules for early-termination penalties.

Optimization levers (concrete items the SEs can suggest to customers to reduce TCO):
1) Quantization & mixed precision profiling: reducing per-token compute by 30–40% for eval workloads—re-profile latency SLOs first.
2) Model sharding + KV cache consolidation: move common prompt prefixes to cached endpoints to reduce active KV working set on GPUs.
3) Pooling across teams: Offer cross-business pooling for burst headroom vs dedicated pods to improve utilization and lower per-token cost.
4) Scheduled batch windows: for batch-heavy workloads, run lower-priority jobs in off-peak windows with preemptible capacity (cloud) or spare cycles (on-prem).
5) Autoscale window tuning: tighten scale-up for latency-critical workloads, extend scale-down aggressiveness to reclaim idle GPUs faster.
6) Host density engineering: for on-prem, evaluate higher-density networking (Mellanox/InfiniBand upgrades) if latency-sensitive; for VPC, prefer instances with NVLink equivalents.

Risk & sensitivity notes (what tilts on-prem vs VPC):
- Heavy egress or data gravity (large datasets inside customer DC) tilts to on-prem.
- Rapid unpredictable growth favors VPC because of elasticity; slow, predictable growth favors on-prem with long amortization.
- Staffing scarcity and high-regulation environments (air-gapped) increase hidden costs of on-prem, captured as risk premium in the model.

Suggested action plan & next steps (practical steps to make this usable in sales conversations):
- Convert the key scenario outputs into a templated 1-page summary PDF (automatically generated from sheet) for each workload profile.
- Create a checklist for SEs to collect inputs (QPS, peak concurrency, average tokens/session, data egress, security constraints) so the sheet can be run quickly during qualification.
- Run a small set of validation calls with 3 existing customers to calibrate colo costs and staffing assumptions (target: validate within 10% of actuals).
- Add knobs to the sheet to toggle advanced optimizations (quantization, pooling) and show incremental ROI for each lever.

Open questions and model improvements (to track):
- Better regional colo cost dataset (APAC numbers need refinement).
- Empirical utilization delta between our dedicated pods vs cloud pooling for similar latency SLOs (instrument with telemetry).
- Incorporate depreciation schedules >36 months for customers with legacy investment.

Notes to self / quick todo (working items):
- Add cell-level comments with explanation for each assumption.
- Link to sample BOM and vendor quotes (Dell, HPE, Lambda) for capex validation.
- Add a simple ROI calculator that highlights customer payback month and NPV delta.

If you want a version tailored to a single customer, drop the following in a pre-sales request: expected peak QPS, average tokens per session, preferred latency P50/P95, existing GPU inventory (if any), and desired support tier. I can produce a one-page comparison for their execs within 48 hours.

-- End of memo (sheet contains the numeric tables and charts referenced above).
